headline: US-Iran conflict escalates as ASX pulls back — Google's record profit and Anthropic's new AI model headline a busy week.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI slipped 2.15% today, likely tracking broader tech weakness on the ASX. The NASDAQ fell 0.64% last night, dragging AI-exposed names lower. Nothing structural has changed — the long-term AI investment theme remains intact.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS dropped another 2.1% today as lithium sentiment stays subdued. The stock is now down nearly 39% from your entry price. Debate continues about when lithium demand will recover, but there's no near-term catalyst in sight.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE fell 1.32% today, reflecting broad pressure on emerging market assets. Rising geopolitical risk (US-Iran conflict, Trump's trade manoeuvring) tends to push investors toward safer havens and away from emerging markets.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG dipped 0.71% today as the ASX 200 slid 0.75% across the board. This is just general market noise — the fund holds a globally diversified mix of growth assets and one soft day changes nothing about its long-term case.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS eased 0.51% today on the ASX, reflecting last night's NASDAQ softness filtering through. The S&P 500 was essentially flat last night, so this is minor. Your VTS position is still slightly in the green overall.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO nudged up 0.61% last night. GTA 6 hype continues to simmer — Take-Two has been actively targeting fake AI-generated leaks ahead of an anticipated new trailer, keeping the title in the news cycle and supporting sentiment.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: GOOG edged up 0.24% last night after posting the biggest quarterly profit in the company's history. There's a nuance though: about two-thirds of that profit came from unrealised investment gains rather than core business cash. Markets took it calmly — the AI spending debate continues.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT was essentially flat last night, up just 0.03%. Microsoft reports earnings this coming week — Azure cloud growth is the key number to watch. Analysts are expecting near 40% growth in Azure, but investors are also watching whether AI infrastructure spending is eating into margins.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Lithium pain continues
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals is down another 2.1% today and sitting 38.6% below your average entry price. There's no near-term recovery catalyst — lithium prices remain depressed and the broader debate about demand timing is unresolved. As a long-term buy-and-hold investor, the question is whether you believe in the EV/battery thematic over a 5–10 year horizon. If yes, sit tight. If conviction has faded, this is worth reassessing honestly.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — Soft session, long-term story intact
watch_today.detail: GXAI dropped 2.15% today tracking NASDAQ weakness. It's now 18% below your entry cost. The AI theme is very much alive — Anthropic just launched Claude Opus 5, Microsoft is cutting AI costs by up to 89% with new in-house models, and GOOG just posted a record profit. This is a structural multi-year bet, not a short-term trade. Hold and let it ride.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Earnings incoming this week
watch_today.detail: Microsoft reports earnings in the coming days (US time). Azure cloud growth near 40% is already expected by the market. The real question is whether AI capex (capital expenditure — money spent building data centres and infrastructure) is starting to pay off. A beat could give MSFT a meaningful lift; a miss or guidance cut could weigh on it. Worth keeping an eye on — but no action needed ahead of the print.

watch_today.title: GOOG — Record profit but watch the detail
watch_today.detail: Google's last reported quarter was its biggest profit ever, but about two-thirds came from unrealised investment gains — meaning paper profits on investments, not cold hard cash from selling ads or cloud services. The core AI investment thesis is strong, and the stock nudged higher last night. Long-term holders should stay put.

watch_today.title: Oil drops 3% — watch inflation implications
watch_today.detail: Crude oil fell sharply last night, down 3.1% to US$89.31/barrel. Cheaper oil is generally good news — it eases inflation pressure, which can reduce the need for interest rate hikes. Worth watching if it continues lower, as it could be a tailwind for consumer spending and equity markets broadly.

watch_today.title: US-Iran conflict — geopolitical risk elevated
watch_today.detail: The US and Iran have been exchanging military strikes on bases across the Middle East. The UN Secretary-General has warned the situation is 'getting out of control'. This kind of escalation typically spooks markets and pushes investors toward gold (which hit US$4,067 last night, up 0.5%) and away from riskier assets. Keep an eye on how this develops over the weekend.

world.summary: The biggest story globally is the US-Iran military conflict escalating across the Middle East, with the UN warning it's getting out of control. At home in the US, the Trump administration is facing lawsuits and internal admissions about using federal funds as political leverage.

stories.title: US and Iran exchange military strikes across the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has been attacking US military bases across the Middle East, and the US has responded with strikes on Iranian targets. The UN Secretary-General has warned the crisis is 'getting out of control.' This is a significant escalation beyond the rhetoric of recent years into actual military exchanges. For everyday Australians, the flow-on effects include oil price volatility (though oil actually fell last night), and broader market uncertainty. The Pentagon has also been caught apparently reducing the published count of US troop deaths on its website, raising transparency concerns.

stories.title: Trump administration admits cancelling clean energy grants to Democratic states
stories.source: The New York Times / The Guardian
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration has officially acknowledged it cancelled clean energy grants specifically to states that did not vote for Trump in the election. Multiple US states have now sued the administration, arguing it's illegal to use federal disaster and energy funds as political punishment. This is a significant constitutional flashpoint — the rule of law around federal funding has rarely been tested this openly. It also signals that US climate and energy policy is being driven by electoral politics rather than policy merit.

stories.title: Trump administration driving to seize control of US election powers
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump White House is reportedly pushing to take control of how elections are administered in the US — a power that has traditionally sat with individual states. Critics say it's creating 'chaos' in the electoral system with legal pushback from states mounting. This is a slow-burn story but a consequential one: if successful, it would represent a fundamental shift in how the world's largest democracy runs its elections. US political instability of this kind can weigh on investor confidence over time.

stories.title: US sends envoys to question Brazil's electoral system
stories.why_it_matters: The US has sent official envoys to Brazil to scrutinise its electoral system, an extraordinary diplomatic move that has raised eyebrows internationally. Brazil held elections in 2022 and its results were contested by then-President Bolsonaro. Critics see this as the Trump administration exporting its election-denialism abroad. It puts significant diplomatic strain on the US-Brazil relationship and reflects a broader pattern of the administration challenging democratic norms both at home and overseas.

stories.title: India emerges as potential alternative to China in global solar supply chain
stories.why_it_matters: As the US and others look to reduce dependence on China for solar panels, India is positioning itself as the key alternative manufacturing hub. Solar panels are the backbone of the global clean energy transition, and China currently dominates their production. A credible Indian alternative would reshape geopolitics around energy, potentially giving Western countries more supply chain security and reducing China's leverage. For Australian investors in clean energy or emerging markets, this is a slow-developing but important structural shift.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 slipped 0.75% today to close at 8,772 — a soft session with no single dramatic catalyst, just general risk-off sentiment as the US-Iran conflict escalates and investors await a big week of US earnings. Last night on Wall Street the S&P 500 was essentially flat (+0.05%) but the NASDAQ dropped 0.64%, dragging tech-exposed ASX names lower today. Gold is holding strong near record highs, oil dropped sharply, and the Aussie dollar edged up slightly.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Essentially flat last night. Markets treading water ahead of a big earnings week.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Tech slipped last night despite Google's strong result — AI spending concerns weighed on sentiment.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold near record highs as investors seek safety amid Middle East tensions.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar nudged up slightly — now very close to the 70 cent mark.

politics.summary: The RBA is back in the spotlight after a strong Australian jobs report reignited talk of another interest rate rise. Critics are hitting out at the RBA's approach, while the data suggests the labour market isn't cooling as fast as hoped.

stories.title: Strong jobs data puts another RBA rate hike back on the table
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's latest employment numbers came in stronger than expected, which is normally good news — but in the current environment it gives the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) reason to keep interest rates high or even lift them again. The RBA has been trying to cool inflation by slowing the economy, and a hot jobs market suggests that isn't happening fast enough. Higher rates mean more expensive mortgages and tougher conditions for borrowers — something many Gold Coast homeowners will feel directly.

stories.title: RBA accused of 'wanting people to lose their jobs'
stories.why_it_matters: Criticism of the RBA's rate strategy is mounting publicly, with commentators arguing the central bank is deliberately engineering job losses to bring inflation down — a harsh but not entirely unfair characterisation of how rate hikes work. When rates rise, businesses invest less and hire less, which pushes unemployment up. The political heat on the RBA is growing just as the jobs data gives it cover to do more. For mortgage holders and anyone in the job market, this debate has very real consequences.

ai.summary: A massive week in AI: Anthropic launched its most powerful model yet (Claude Opus 5), Microsoft revealed new in-house AI models that slash costs by up to 89%, and a big industry fight over how — or whether — to regulate AI is heating up in Washington.

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Opus 5 — its most capable model yet
stories.why_it_matters: Anthropic has officially released Claude Opus 5, its flagship AI model. According to CNBC, the model rivals the best offerings from OpenAI and Google, and crucially it's being positioned as cheaper for businesses to run — a key selling point as companies worry about AI costs blowing out. The timing is notable: it lands just as Microsoft is also slashing AI costs, meaning the 'efficiency vs raw power' battle in AI is accelerating fast. For anyone using AI tools at work, more capable and cheaper models are coming quickly.

stories.title: Microsoft launches in-house AI models — cuts costs up to 89% vs OpenAI
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft has quietly built its own AI models that it says are up to 89% cheaper to run than equivalent OpenAI models. This is a big deal — Microsoft has invested billions in OpenAI but is now building alternatives, suggesting it wants to reduce its dependency (and costs). For businesses using Microsoft's AI products (Azure, Copilot), this could mean significantly lower bills. It also puts more competitive pressure on OpenAI and signals that the age of expensive AI is ending faster than many expected.

stories.title: Nvidia and 24 companies back open-weights AI — but Google, OpenAI and Anthropic stay out
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia and 24 other tech companies have signed a letter supporting 'open-weights' AI — meaning AI models where the underlying code is publicly available, similar to open-source software. Notably absent: OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, who all keep their most powerful models closed. This is the AI industry's version of a values split: open models let anyone build on top of them (great for innovation, potentially risky for safety), while closed models give the big labs control. Washington is weighing in too, considering a ban on Chinese AI models, which is driving some of this lobbying activity.

stories.title: AI regulation debate heats up — efficiency vs safety
stories.why_it_matters: There are now two loud camps in the AI regulation debate: one arguing that heavy rules will kill the productivity gains AI offers (Australia's Canberra Times weighed in on this side), and another citing new research warning that weak rules actually make AI less safe — not because of sci-fi risks, but because poorly governed systems get deployed in high-stakes environments without adequate testing. The White House has set an August 1 deadline for an AI policy review. The outcome matters for how fast AI gets deployed into healthcare, legal, financial and government services — sectors that affect all of us.

sport.summary: A big NRL Round 21 weekend underway — the Raiders demolished the Tigers 56-10, the Roosters edged the Knights in a thriller, and Rabbitohs upset the Storm. There's a nasty injury cloud over the Knights heading into the back end of the season. In AFL, Geelong beat Melbourne at the MCG but the win was soured by controversy.

stories.title: Raiders demolish Wests Tigers 56-10 in Round 21 blowout
stories.why_it_matters: Canberra Raiders put on a clinic against Wests Tigers at GIO Stadium today, running out 56-10 winners in one of the most one-sided results of Round 21. The 46-point margin is a massive statement from Canberra as the finals race heats up, while the Tigers' season continues to fall apart. The Cowboys vs Broncos Queensland derby is still to come tonight.

stories.title: Roosters pip Knights 23-22 in Friday night thriller — injury cloud over Newcastle
stories.why_it_matters: The Roosters held on to beat the Knights 23-22 in a tight Friday night game at McDonald Jones Stadium. The result was overshadowed by injury news out of Newcastle — Fox Sports reported a 'double knightmare blow' with their $13 million man going down during the match. The Knights are already battling for finals contention and losing key personnel at this stage of the season is a serious blow.

stories.title: Rabbitohs upset Melbourne Storm 28-26 in Friday night thriller
stories.why_it_matters: South Sydney Rabbitohs knocked off the Melbourne Storm 28-26 at Accor Stadium on Friday night in a genuine thriller. The win is a big deal for the Rabbitohs, who needed the two points to keep their finals campaign alive. For Melbourne, it's a rare slip-up that could have ladder implications with the finals approaching. Bulldogs vs Warriors is currently at half-time (Bulldogs leading 12-0), with the Cowboys-Broncos Queensland derby still to come tonight.

stories.title: Geelong beat Melbourne at MCG but 'worst rule in history' sparks AFL furore
stories.why_it_matters: Geelong broke Melbourne's impressive MCG winning streak with a gutsy victory, but the post-match headlines were dominated by controversy over a rule application that the AFL world — including Geelong supporters — called 'abhorrent' and the 'worst rule in history.' Collingwood also won this week, with coach Craig McRae airing a post-game complaint despite the victory. With Geelong facing multiple injury concerns ahead of a clash with the hot Magpies, the Cats' finals preparation has some nervous energy around it.
